messages.body_plain:
Hi Mike,

Just a quick question: I have calibrated the tree based on the literature but I´m not sure if what I did is acceptable for each specimen. I have created a tree with all specimens, and collapsed within species.

First, I tried to use branch length = 0 for each specimen but it doesn´t worked fine as the time plot was not as expected. Thus, I have used a branch length of 0.5 for each specimen and it worked fine.

There are wrong implications while performing the analysis in this way?

Thank you so much in advance,

Gui

Em sex., 19 de jun. de 2020 às 11:27, Mike Collyer <mlco...@gmail.com> escreveu:

> Gui,
>
> You can only connect a tree to tips in your plot if you have one value per species.  Even though a tree in phylogenetics describes the evolutionary relationships among species, a tree in a statistical sense does not make sense there are N tips for N species.  You have to either come up with a tree that describes the relationship among individuals within species, in addition to species, or collapse your data into species values (perhaps find the means by species).

Gui,

first, as Mike said in his previous email, comparative methods are designed to work with species (and their associated phylogeny), not specimens. Many of them will not work unless you have branch lengths >0 for all your branches (don´t allow polytomies or 0 terminal branches).

Second, if I understand correctly, in this case you are partially "inventing" some branches. Whether 0.5 of branch length is long or short should be put in the context of the rest of the tree length. If you are convinced that this is the approach you want to take, make sure to use proportionally very short branches for adding individuals within species, but be aware that this is what I called "invented".

I would be quite sceptical of this kind of approach, but it´s up to you. Again, as Mike suggested, I think it would be much more adequate that you work at the species level, describing species by the mean (or some other value) of your specimens, but it all depends on your biological question and system.

Hope this helps

Antigoni

> Gui,

> first, as Mike said in his previous email, comparative methods are designed to work with species (and their associated phylogeny), not specimens. Many of them will not work unless you have branch lengths >0 for all your branches (don´t allow polytomies or 0 terminal branches).
>
> Second, if I understand correctly, in this case you are partially "inventing" some branches. Whether 0.5 of branch length is long or short should be put in the context of the rest of the tree length. If you are convinced that this is the approach you want to take, make sure to use proportionally very short branches for adding individuals within species, but be aware that this is what I called "invented".
>
> I would be quite sceptical of this kind of approach, but it´s up to you. Again, as Mike suggested, I think it would be much more adequate that you work at the species level, describing species by the mean (or some other value) of your specimens, but it all depends on your biological question and system.
>
> Hope this helps
>
> Antigoni

Dear Dr. Adams,

That makes a lot of sense. Thank you for your help.

Sincerely,
Russell

On Tuesday, June 30, 2020 at 2:33:46 PM UTC-4, Adams, Dean [EEOB] wrote:

> Hi Russell,
>
>
>
> Procedurally, one could use a set of additional landmarks on the mandible (or a horizontal), perform GPA, and then remove the additional non-symphysis landmarks. This will retain the orientation of the symphysis relative to the rest of the mandible in the set of aligned coordinates representing the symphysis (note: I’d use actual landmarks on the mandible not some arbitrary horizontal. That goes back to the days of the Frankfurt plane in anthropology which ended up having about as many challenges as it solved).
>
>
>
> However, understand that when doing such things, one is no longer doing a shape analysis, and interpretation of any patterns becomes exceedingly complicated. In essence, the symphysis landmarks extracted from a larger configuration of points have a shape and now a ‘relative’ orientation; which is what your post seemed to wish to retain. However, they also do not have constant size, so there are size differences, and there are positional differences (the full configuration is centered, but that does not guarantee that the symphyses are). So in gaining the ability to retain the orientation one must now also explain which part of the observed variation is due to shape differences, size differences, orientation differences, and positional differences. Thus while procedurally possible, I don’t see this as advancing one’s explanatory power of anatomical variation.
>
>
>
> I see two paths forward. One is to use additional landmarks on the rest of the mandible, perform GPA and shape analyses, but focus one’s interpretation on what is happening with respect to the symphysis. Also, adding some analyses of the symphysis relative to the rest of the mandible (e.g., PLS) might be very important in identifying whether any differences in shape/position of the symphysis are correlated with mandibular shape changes.
>
>
> A second approach would be to use only the symphysis, and translate and scale them only (no standardizing of orientation). This is again technically possible, but only makes sense if the mandibles are in an absolute standard position: something we can never attain (yes, this goes back to problems with the Frankfurt plane and others and why we developed GPA in the first place).
>

par(mar = c(5, 4, 4, 2) + 0.1)

Just to follow up on Dean’s suggestion, the text function has an argument, pos, for the position of the label with respect to the points, where 1 = below, 2 = to the left, 3 = above, and 4 = to the right.  There is an argument, offset, to define the distance away from the point to add the label.  (see ?text to learn more.)  These or the way Dean demonstrated — more direct programming — give the user unlimited control over how to make their plots.  The old plotTangentSpace took this kind of control away.

Ideally plotting in R takes advantage of the base plotting system, which allows users to use any of the plotting tools available in R to manipulate plots.  The old plotTangentSpace function did not allow this, and it caused users all kinds of problems when they wanted to make quality plots for publications.  (One of the worse emails to receive was someone who had a paper accepted but had to come up with a better quality plot when they submitted a plotTangentSpace plot as a figure…)  With any geomorph plot, you should be able to change the points, change colors, add text, add points, add arrows, etc., and use bmp, tiff, jpeg, pdf, or png functions to save high-resolution copies of plots.

One “bonus” the old plotTangentSpace function had was that it absolved users from essential plotting skills in R, which is historically unfortunate.  If data analysis in R is preferred, then acquiring some plotting skill in R should also be a goal.  Some people prefer advanced plotting with ggplot2 and geomorph plots should be quite amenable to using ggplot2.  In Dean’s example, if it were changed to this:

pca.plot <- plot(PCA, main = "PCA”)

then pca.plot$plot.args would have the plotting parameters one might wish to use and change in a ggplot approach.

> data(plethspecies)

axis2

> Just to follow up on Dean’s suggestion, the text function has an argument, pos, for the position of the label with respect to the points, where 1 = below, 2 = to the left, 3 = above, and 4 = to the right.  There is an argument, offset, to define the distance away from the point to add the label.  (see ?text to learn more.)  These or the way Dean demonstrated — more direct programming — give the user unlimited control over how to make their plots.  The old plotTangentSpace took this kind of control away.
>
> Ideally plotting in R takes advantage of the base plotting system, which allows users to use any of the plotting tools available in R to manipulate plots.  The old plotTangentSpace function did not allow this, and it caused users all kinds of problems when they wanted to make quality plots for publications.  (One of the worse emails to receive was someone who had a paper accepted but had to come up with a better quality plot when they submitted a plotTangentSpace plot as a figure…)  With any geomorph plot, you should be able to change the points, change colors, add text, add points, add arrows, etc., and use bmp, tiff, jpeg, pdf, or png functions to save high-resolution copies of plots.
>
> One “bonus” the old plotTangentSpace function had was that it absolved users from essential plotting skills in R, which is historically unfortunate.  If data analysis in R is preferred, then acquiring some plotting skill in R should also be a goal.  Some people prefer advanced plotting with ggplot2 and geomorph plots should be quite amenable to using ggplot2.  In Dean’s example, if it were changed to this:

I can see using the latter that a shape change is occurring, and I would like to express the shape difference in a p-value to accompany my images. The numbers of specimens in my NP and LSA pops are not the same.

Would the correct code look something like this?
> t.test(pca.NP$pc.scores[,1], pca.LSA$pc.scores[,1], var.equal = T)

>  t.test(pca.NP$pc.scores[,2], pca.LSA$pc.scores[,2], var.equal = T)

Am I correct in understanding that this will tell me if a statistical difference exists between my two populations relative to PC1 and PC2?

Thanks for your time and help,
Sean

messages.body_plain:
Sean,

generally speaking you could use a t-test to compare the PC scores between two samples and get a pvalue out of it. I see, however, several drawbacks with your approach:

1) You are assuming in your code that equal variances occur between your samples (i.e. argument var.equal = T), which does not need be the case (this would need to be confirmed)

2) From your code it looks like you have performed PCA separately for the two samples you are trying to compare (NP and LSA). This makes the produced variables (PCs) not comensurate and thus not comparable, as they might (and probably WILL) have different compositions. This is plain wrong, it is like comparing the length of one population to the width of the other.

3) Most importantly for shape analyses, it is a pity and completely unnecessary to limit your inferences to PCs. PCA is a very useful approach for visualizing multidimensional data (would still need to be a single PCA with ALL your observations, though!). But your analytical procedures need not be limited to whatever % of variance a PCA captures. In fact, this might be misleading, as differences in shape between your groups may still exist, although not in PC1 and PC2. I recommend, instead, that you run a permutation-based ANOVA comparison as implemented in the function procD.lm using the entire variation in shape space.

Hope this helps

Antigoni

> Sean,
>
> generally speaking you could use a t-test to compare the PC scores between two samples and get a pvalue out of it. I see, however, several drawbacks with your approach:
>
> 1) You are assuming in your code that equal variances occur between your samples (i.e. argument var.equal = T), which does not need be the case (this would need to be confirmed)
>
> 2) From your code it looks like you have performed PCA separately for the two samples you are trying to compare (NP and LSA). This makes the produced variables (PCs) not comensurate and thus not comparable, as they might (and probably WILL) have different compositions. This is plain wrong, it is like comparing the length of one population to the width of the other.
>
> 3) Most importantly for shape analyses, it is a pity and completely unnecessary to limit your inferences to PCs. PCA is a very useful approach for visualizing multidimensional data (would still need to be a single PCA with ALL your observations, though!). But your analytical procedures need not be limited to whatever % of variance a PCA captures. In fact, this might be misleading, as differences in shape between your groups may still exist, although not in PC1 and PC2. I recommend, instead, that you run a permutation-based ANOVA comparison as implemented in the function procD.lm using the entire variation in shape space.
>
> Hope this helps
>
> Antigoni
